effect_estimate.comment: Note minor internal discrepancy in the paper's reporting of the +24.8% ATT: Abstract (p. 1) and Conclusion (p. 15) refer to a 24.8% improvement in toilet functionality, whereas Section 3.7 (p. 9) and Table 8 (p. 10) report +24.8% for water source functionality and +19.3% for toilet usage rate. Qualitative findings showed effects depended on meaningful rather than tokenistic participation.
effect_estimate.value: In propensity score matching (N = 400 households across 16 villages), active/meaningful women's participation in Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) increased water source functionality by +24.8% (SE = 5.2, t = 4.77, p < 0.001, 95% CI [14.6%, 35.0%]; cited in Abstract/Conclusion as toilet functionality), increased toilet usage rate by +19.3% (SE = 4.7, t = 4.11, p < 0.001, 95% CI [10.1%, 28.5%]), reduced daily water collection time by -31.4 min (SE = 8.6, t = -3.65, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-48.3, -14.5]), reduced diarrhoeal illness incidence by -12.7% (SE = 3.8, t = -3.34, p = 0.001, 95% CI [-20.2%, -5.2%]), and reduced menstrual hygiene management (MHM) constraints by -18.2% (SE = 4.9, t = -3.71, p < 0.001, 95% CI [-27.8%, -8.6%]). In probit regression, VWSC awareness campaigns increased consistent toilet usage probability by 0.158 (SE = 0.047, z = 3.36, p = 0.001, 95% CI [0.066, 0.250]), while in logistic regression low women's agency score (<5 on a 0-10 VWSC participation index) increased odds of water-borne illness (Adjusted OR = 1.62, 95% CI [1.07, 2.46], p = 0.023, marginal effect +10.4%); women's agency correlated negatively with the multidimensional Gender-WASH Inequality Index (GWII = 0.357 overall; r = -0.52), with voice deficit accounting for 22.4% of overall GWII.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 7-10, Sections 3.3-3.7 & Tables 4, 5, 7, 8; PDF p. 15, Section 5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by mixed-methods/cross-sectional design ceiling (authors explicitly note in Section 4.6 that the cross-sectional design constrains causal inference despite PSM). Rated 2 because the governance/participatory mechanism—women's attendance, speaking time, decision-making influence, and leadership in VWSCs prioritizing water availability, cleanliness, privacy, and maintenance—was directly observed via participant observation of VWSC and Gram Sabha meetings, 16 FGDs, and 32 KIIs alongside household survey regressions.

sample_size.comment: Multi-stage systematic random household survey across 4 districts (2 blocks per district, 2 villages per block = 16 villages; 94.3% response rate yielding 400 households, with N = 217 households in the menstrual hygiene management sub-analysis), plus purposively sampled qualitative FGDs, KIIs, and committee meeting observations.
sample_size.value: 400 rural households across 16 villages in 4 districts (100 per district, 25 per village; including 217 households with menstruating members in MHM sub-analysis); 16 focus group discussions (8 women-only, 4 men-only, 4 mixed); 32 key informant interviews; participant observation of VWSC and Gram Sabha meetings
